title: The Soul Loosed in Sickness: A Typology of Mystical Seeing
arc: The teaching describes men in whom, during a brief sickness, the soul is loosed forth from the body so that the body's eye "blossoms" into mystical sight; it then sorts these seers into kinds — those whose soul departs and returns in one and the same hour, those who linger longer before coming back to their feet, and groupings of seven and three — distinguishing what each kind glimpses in the Deep or in the Light.
reading:
This chapter is severely lacunose, but enough survives to see its shape. Its subject, given by the title, is the phenomenon of men whose bodily eye "blossoms forth" — that is, whose ordinary natural understanding is opened beyond itself into a moment of mystical seeing. In Swedenborgian terms the teaching is treating that condition in which, during sickness or near-death, the bonds tying soul to body slacken and the soul's interior senses are briefly opened into the spiritual world. The opening words confirm this setting: the experience comes "in a sickness for a little while," and concerns "men who habitually" undergo it. The body itself does not die; the soul is "loosed forth" (ⲃⲁⲗⲉ ⲁⲃⲁⲗ) from its natural binding for a measured interval and then returns.

The teaching's argument moves by way of a typology. It distinguishes several kinds of such seers by the manner and duration of the loosening. One class is described as undergoing the whole motion — the soul going forth and the soul returning — within "one and the same hour": a brief, complete circuit in which a man falls into sickness, his soul slips its body, sees, and comes back almost at once. Against these are set "yet others, who habitually" experience the loosening differently: they "abide delaying," they tarry in the loosed state, and "delay coming at their foot" — that is, they are slow to return to standing in the natural body. The foot, as the ultimate of the natural, is the place of re-entry; these seers are slow to set the soul down again into ultimates.

Between these two extremes the surviving phrases sketch a more elaborate ordering. There is mention of "the [place] in which the names habitually release forth" — apparently a state in which the names of souls are called and unbound, the moment of summons that draws the soul upward. The repeated formula "in this manner..." (ⲙⲡⲣⲏⲧⲉ) governs paralleled descriptions, so that two or three modes of release are being set side by side. Twice the word ⲛⲟⲩⲛ, the Deep, surfaces: some of these soul-departures evidently descend toward the hells and behold what is there, while other passages mention "the light" and "taking to the light" and the cosmos seen as if from outside. So the typology is also a sorting by direction: some seers are shown the Deep, others the Light, according to the quality of soul that goes forth.

Toward the close, the teaching gathers numbers — "seven men of..." and "this other three" — which in the project's vocabulary read as fullness in ultimates (seven) and fullness of process (three). The teaching is therefore not anecdotal but doctrinal: it is laying out the complete set of orderly ways in which the loosening of soul from body can occur, the seven-fold rank of those whose vision touches ultimates and the three-fold rank of a further class. The phrase "who has also reached this man... the hour when they..." suggests that each class is keyed to an appointed hour at which the awakening Call reaches the man and his soul is permitted to rise.

Read as a whole, then, the teaching belongs to the chapter's larger doctrine of the soul as captive light momentarily released. Sickness is the occasion in which the natural's grip on the soul weakens; the body's eye, normally closed to the spiritual, blossoms; and what the soul perceives in that opening — whether the Deep below or the light above, whether briefly within an hour or at length until the names are released — depends on the man's state. The chapter is teaching its hearers to recognize that such mystical seeings are real, are ordered, are differentiated by spiritual quality, and belong to the Lord's larger work of drawing souls outward from the body's binding so that, whether by glimpse or by sustained vision, the soul may be turned toward the Light. Because so much of the text is gone, the precise content of each class — what exactly the seven see, what the three see, what falls "from" what — cannot be recovered with confidence; but the structural argument (sickness → loosening → seeing → ordered classes of seers) is clearly the teaching's spine.
